title: Gravitation
summary: Objects thrown up come back and fruits fall from trees because the earth attracts them. Newton realised (the story of the falling apple) that the same force keeps the moon moving around the earth and the planets around the sun. This gravitational force exists everywhere in the universe, acts between all objects and is always attractive.

Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them; the force acts along the line joining them: F = G m1m2/r². G is the universal gravitational constant, the same everywhere: 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Because G is so small, the force between ordinary objects (two students 1 m apart) is extremely weak, but between huge bodies (earth and moon, about 2 × 10²⁰ N) it is very large. If the distance is doubled the force becomes one-fourth; if it is halved the force becomes four times; if both masses are doubled it becomes four times. The earth's gravitational force is called gravity.

A falling body speeds up because of gravity; this acceleration is g. A coin and a crumpled paper ball dropped together land together, and in a vacuum (Boyle's experiment) a coin and a feather fall together — air resistance alone slows a flat paper. So g does not depend on the mass of the falling body. From mg = GMm/R², g = GM/R², where M is the mass and R the radius of the earth. With M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻²; its SI unit is m s⁻². g is slightly more at the poles than at the equator because the earth's radius is smaller there; on the moon it is about one-sixth of that on earth.

The equations of uniformly accelerated motion apply with a replaced by g: v = u + gt; s = ut + ½gt²; v² = u² + 2gs. g is taken as negative for upward motion. Example: a ball that rises 122.5 m was thrown up at u = √(2 × 9.8 × 122.5) = 49 m/s and takes 49/9.8 = 5 s to reach the top (and 10 s to come back).

Mass is the quantity of matter in a body; it is the same everywhere (earth, moon or space), measures inertia and is measured with a pan balance in kilograms. Weight is the force with which the earth attracts a body: W = mg, measured in newtons with a spring balance; it acts vertically downward and varies from place to place with g. Example: a 20 kg body weighs 20 × 9.8 = 196 N; a body weighing 78.4 N has mass 78.4/9.8 = 8 kg.

A weighing machine shows the reaction of the floor on our body. If the person and the machine both fall freely with acceleration g, the person presses nothing and the machine reads zero. So a body falling freely under gravity is weightless — this is why astronauts in an orbiting spacecraft (which is falling freely around the earth) float. We feel lighter in a lift accelerating downward and heavier in one accelerating upward.

A wooden block pushed under water springs back up, and a mug of water feels lighter inside a bucket: a fluid (liquid or gas) exerts an upward force called the buoyant force or upthrust. A stone hung from a spring balance shows a smaller reading as it is lowered into water, and the reading stops changing once it is fully immersed. There is no buoyant force in a vacuum.

Archimedes' principle: when a body is immersed fully or partly in a fluid, it experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it. The buoyant force depends on the density of the fluid and the volume of the body immersed. A body sinks if its weight is more than the buoyant force (a stone displaces water weighing less than itself) and floats if the buoyant force equals its weight (a wooden block). Example: a body weighing 5.0 N in air and 2.5 N in water has a buoyant force of 2.5 N. Applications: designing ships and submarines, hydrometers (density of liquids) and lactometers (purity of milk).

objective: Read the passage and answer: 'Archimedes' principle states that when an object is fully or partially immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. Whether it sinks or floats depends on how its weight compares with the buoyant force.' (1) A stone sinks in water. Which statement explains this? (a) The stone displaces water weighing less than itself (b) The buoyant force is greater than its weight (c) Water pushes it up strongly (d) It weighs the same as the displaced water. (2) A wooden block floats on water. What does this tell you about the buoyant force on it? (a) less than its weight (b) equal to its weight (c) greater than its weight (d) no relation
(1) (a) — the water it displaces weighs less than the stone. (2) (b) — the buoyant force equals the weight of the block.

Read the passage on Newton's law of gravitation (F = G m1m2/r², where G is the universal gravitational constant) and answer: (1) How does the force change if the distance between two bodies is doubled? (2) Write the value of G in SI units.
(1) It becomes one-fourth (F ∝ 1/r²). (2) G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

case.passage: Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle. The earth's attraction gives every falling body the same acceleration, g, which near the earth's surface is about 9.8 m s⁻² and is given by g = GM/R², where M is the mass and R the radius of the earth. Because g is constant near the surface, the equations of uniformly accelerated motion can be used for falling bodies with a replaced by g. The weight of a body, W = mg, therefore depends on where the body is, while its mass does not.

vsa: State Newton's law of gravitation. How does the force of gravitation between two objects change when the distance between them is reduced to half?

Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them (F = Gm1m2/r²). If the distance is halved, the force becomes 1/(½)² = 4 times.
Mass of an object is constant at all places but its weight varies from place to place. Explain.

Mass is the quantity of matter in a body, which does not change with place. Weight is the force of gravity on it, W = mg; since g varies from place to place (more at the poles, less at the equator, about one-sixth on the moon), the weight also varies.
State Archimedes' principle. Write two applications.

When a body is immersed fully or partly in a fluid, it experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it. Applications: designing ships and submarines; hydrometers and lactometers.
What is meant by buoyant force? State the factors on which the buoyant force acting on a body at a given place depends.
The upward force exerted by a fluid on a body immersed in it is the buoyant force (upthrust). It depends on (1) the density of the fluid and (2) the volume of the body immersed in the fluid.
State Archimedes' principle. What is the condition for a body to float in a liquid?

A body immersed fully or partly in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. A body floats when the weight of the liquid it displaces (the buoyant force) equals its own weight, i.e. its density is less than that of the liquid.
Why does a paratrooper use a parachute to descend slowly after jumping from a height?

Without a parachute he would fall freely with acceleration g and hit the ground at a dangerous speed. The large parachute meets a large air resistance (and upthrust of air), which balances most of his weight, so he comes down slowly and safely.

or: An object falls from a height and reaches the ground in 0.5 s (g = 10 m s⁻²). (a) With what speed does it strike the ground? (b) What is its average speed during the 0.5 s? (c) From what height was it dropped?

sa: What is the magnitude of the gravitational force between the earth and a 1 kg object on its surface? (Mass of the earth = 6 × 10²⁴ kg, radius = 6.4 × 10⁶ m)
F = GMm/R² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6 × 10²⁴ × 1)/(6.4 × 10⁶)² ≈ 9.8 N — which is the weight of the 1 kg object.

sa.note: April 2025 asked the same for a 5 kg object: F ≈ 49 N.

sa: A stone is dropped from the top of a 40 m high tower. Calculate its speed after 2 s. Also find the speed with which it strikes the ground. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
After 2 s: v = u + gt = 0 + 9.8 × 2 = 19.6 m/s. On striking the ground: v² = u² + 2gh = 2 × 9.8 × 40 = 784, so v = 28 m/s.
(a) State Archimedes' principle and two applications. (b) Explain why a paratrooper opens the parachute immediately after jumping from a flying aeroplane.

(a) A body immersed fully or partly in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. Applications: ships and submarines; hydrometers and lactometers. (b) The open parachute meets a large air resistance, which reduces his acceleration so that he falls slowly and lands safely instead of hitting the ground at high speed.

(a) Two metal spheres, each of mass 200 g, have radii 4 cm and 10 cm. How will the ratio of their weights differ when weighed in water and in vacuum? (b) A cricket ball thrown vertically upward at 49 m/s is caught at the point of throw. Find the total time taken.

(a) In vacuum both weigh the same (ratio 1 : 1). In water the larger sphere displaces much more water, so it has a larger buoyant force and appears lighter; the smaller sphere appears heavier, so the ratio is no longer 1 : 1. (b) Time to rise: t = u/g = 49/9.8 = 5 s; it takes the same time to fall, so total time = 10 s.
la: (a) State Archimedes' principle. (b) What are the two factors on which the buoyant force acting on a body depends? (c) Does the buoyant force act on a body kept in a vacuum? (d) A body weighs 5.0 N in air and 2.5 N when immersed in water. Find the buoyant force.

(a) When a body is immersed wholly or partly in a fluid, it experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by it. (b) The density of the fluid and the volume of the body immersed in it. (c) No — there is no fluid to be displaced, so there is no upthrust. (d) Buoyant force = loss in weight = 5.0 − 2.5 = 2.5 N.

State Newton's law of gravitation. Derive an expression for the acceleration due to gravity on the earth's surface. Why do a heavy and a light object dropped together reach the ground at the same time?

Every particle attracts every other with a force F = Gm1m2/r². For a body of mass m on the earth's surface, the force of gravity is mg and also GMm/R², so mg = GMm/R², giving g = GM/R², where M and R are the earth's mass and radius. This expression does not contain m, so every body, heavy or light, falls with the same acceleration g (≈ 9.8 m s⁻²); they reach the ground together if air resistance is negligible (a coin and a feather fall together in a vacuum).
